_about: Step-by-step process manuals (roadmap item 4). scripts/build_manuals.py renders each manual three ways: site/manuals/<id>.html (web, prints to PDF), docs/manuals/<id>.md (GitHub) and the README block between the manuals markers, plus site/manuals.html (the shelf). Never hand-edit those outputs. Builder text is for beginners; 'spec' is the engineer handbook (operation specification) and 'deep' is process-engineer depth. Every number carries [@key] from references.json. Frames describe an isometric picture: 'layers' bottom to top (h in px, optional segs as [from, to] in % of width, new=true highlights what this step adds) and 'props' are drawn on top. Safety tiers as in fab_steps.json: 0 safe, 1 care, 2 equipment or heat, 3 institution-only chemistry (no parameters published).

manuals.title: Grow the crystal and cut the wafer
manuals.subtitle: Czochralski growth: melt, seed, neck, body, grind, slice, polish, sort
manuals.intro: Every chip starts as one perfect crystal. Ultra-pure silicon is melted with a pinch of dopant, a seed crystal is dipped in and slowly pulled up, and the melt freezes onto it atom by atom in the seed’s own arrangement. The ingot is then ground, sliced into wafers and polished to a mirror. The dopant does not freeze in evenly, which is why resistivity changes along the ingot.
manuals.model_after: Dopant along the ingot follows the Scheil equation [@scheil1942] with segregation coefficients from Trumbore [@trumbore1960] and the effective-k theory of Burton, Prim and Slichter [@bps1953], as in the Fab Journey’s crystal theatre; crystal pulling follows Czochralski [@czochralski1918], Teal and Little [@teal1950] and Dash [@dash1959]; wafer practice follows Plummer, Deal and Griffin [@plummer2000].

you_need.label: Grinder, wire saw, polisher, four-point probe

steps.title: Melt the silicon and add the dopant
steps.do: Load polysilicon into a quartz crucible, add the dopant and melt it all under argon. The melt is doped richer than the target, because the crystal will take in only a fraction k of it.
steps.check: Melt temperature steady; dopant weight logged.

chips.t: the crystal takes in only a fraction k of the dopant [@bps1953]
boron k ≈ 0.8, phosphorus k ≈ 0.35 [@trumbore1960]

spec.purpose: Make a melt that freezes to the target resistivity
spec.control: Charge weight, dopant weight, melt temperature
spec.ooc: Wrong dopant weight: the ingot misses its resistivity and is sold to a looser spec

steps.deep: The melt is doped to N_seed / k so that the first part of the crystal hits the target. Silicon melts at about 1414 °C, so the puller is a staff-run, water-cooled furnace [@plummer2000].

steps.title: Dip the seed and pull a thin neck
steps.do: Lower a small seed crystal of the chosen orientation into the melt, let it wet, then pull a thin neck before widening.
steps.check: The neck is thin and even; the meniscus is stable.

chips.t: a thin neck lets dislocations grow out: dislocation-free silicon [@dash1959]
the seed sets the orientation of the whole ingot, (100) for MOS [@plummer2000]

spec.control: Seed rotation, pull speed, neck diameter
spec.ooc: Dislocations in the neck: melt back and dip again

steps.deep: The thermal shock of dipping makes dislocations in the seed. Pulling a thin, fast neck lets them run out to the surface and vanish, so the ingot above it grows free of them, as Dash showed in 1959 [@dash1959].

steps.title: Pull the body
steps.do: Widen to the full diameter, then pull the crystal slowly upward while seed and crucible turn in opposite directions.
steps.check: Diameter on target along the whole body.

chips.t: a slower pull or a cooler melt makes the crystal wider [@plummer2000]
the dopant piles up in the melt, so resistivity falls along the ingot [@scheil1942]

spec.control: Pull rate, rotation, melt temperature, diameter camera
spec.ooc: Diameter swing: the controller adjusts pull rate and heater power

steps.deep: As the crystal grows, the interface rejects a fraction 1 − k of the dopant back into the shrinking melt, so the melt and the next slice of crystal get richer. The solid follows C_s = kC₀(1 − f)^(k−1), where f is the fraction already frozen [@scheil1942]. Stirring and pull rate shift the effective k [@bps1953].

steps.title: Grind and mark the orientation
steps.do: Grind the ingot to an exact diameter and cut a notch or flat along it that marks the crystal orientation.
steps.check: Diameter and notch position within tolerance.

chips.t: the notch tells every later tool which way the crystal faces [@plummer2000]

spec.purpose: Make every wafer the same size and orientation
spec.ooc: Notch misplaced: regrind or downgrade

steps.deep: Lithography and etching depend on the crystal planes, so every wafer carries its orientation with it. X-ray diffraction finds the planes before the notch is ground [@plummer2000].

steps.title: Slice, flatten and polish
steps.do: Saw the ingot into thin wafers, remove the sawing damage and polish one face to a mirror.
steps.check: Thickness, flatness and surface meet the spec.

chips.t: the damage-removal etch is institution-only chemistry
the final polish is chemical-mechanical, like planarization [@plummer2000]

spec.purpose: Turn the ingot into flat, mirror-smooth wafers
spec.ooc: Scratches or haze: repolish; warp: reject

steps.deep: Sawing leaves a damaged layer that would crack and trap impurities, so it is lapped and chemically etched away before the polish. The etch chemistry stays with the wafer maker [@plummer2000].

steps.title: Measure and sort
steps.do: Measure resistivity at points along the ingot and on each wafer. Wafers inside the customer’s band are prime; the rest go to looser uses.
steps.check: Resistivity within the band; no dislocations or particles.

chips.t: resistivity falls from seed to tail for any k below 1 [@scheil1942]
resistivity comes from doping through the mobility [@caughey1967]

spec.purpose: Keep only wafers that meet the spec
spec.ooc: Out of band: sold to a looser spec or recycled

steps.deep: Only part of each ingot stays inside a tight resistivity band; the crystal theatre shows how much for each dopant and tolerance. Resistivity follows ρ = 1/(qμN) with the mobility falling as doping rises [@caughey1967].

variant.title: From a metals experiment to 300 mm wafers
variant.lead: A method for measuring how fast metals crystallise became the start of every chip.

facts.t: Czochralski pulled metal crystals from a melt in 1918 to measure crystallisation speed
Teal and Little pulled single crystals of germanium at Bell Labs in 1950
Dash’s thin neck gave dislocation-free silicon in 1959
Boron’s segregation coefficient is about 0.8, phosphorus’s about 0.35

variant.safety: Crystal pullers hold molten silicon above 1400 °C under argon and are run only by trained staff; the damage-removal etch uses institution-only chemistry.

leave_out: Dopant follows the Scheil equation with one effective k; real pulls vary it with pull rate and stirring.
Oxygen from the quartz crucible, which every Czochralski wafer contains, is described, not modelled.
Float-zone growth and silicon-on-insulator wafers are left out.
No etch chemistry or furnace setting is given: the puller and the etch are staff-run.

manuals.title: Clean the wafer before every furnace
manuals.subtitle: Wafer cleaning, explained conceptually: count, remove films, oxide, particles and metals, rinse and count again
manuals.route: Every route: before each oxidation, diffusion and deposition
manuals.next: Manual 4B · Photomask, or straight into a furnace step
manuals.intro: A wafer that looks spotless still carries oily films, a thin skin of oxide, dust and single metal atoms. Any of them can ruin a transistor: a particle bridges two lines, a trace of iron kills the electrons that should carry current. Fabs clean before every hot step. The chemistry is institution-only, so this manual shows what each stage removes and why, never how to mix or handle anything.
manuals.model_after: The stages follow Kern’s cleaning sequence and his review of how it evolved [@kern1970] [@kern1990]; particle sizes and killer defects follow Stapper [@stapper1983]; iron in silicon follows Istratov and co-workers [@istratov1999]. The cleaning theatre computes what is left after each stage.

you_need.label: Wafer arriving from the last step
Wet bench run by trained staff

steps.title: Count what is on the wafer
steps.do: Scan the wafer with a laser particle counter before it is cleaned. Every speck that scatters light is logged with its size and place.
steps.check: The count and the map go on the traveler.

chips.t: small particles far outnumber large ones [@stapper1983]
a map shows where they came from

spec.control: Particles per wafer above the inspection size
spec.ooc: Count far above normal: look for the tool that added them

steps.deep: Particle sizes follow roughly an inverse cube law, so most of the count is small particles. What matters is how many are larger than the narrowest line, the killer size, because those can short or break a wire [@stapper1983].

steps.title: Remove organic films
steps.do: The first bath turns oily films from resist, handling and the air into gas. They would otherwise shield everything underneath from the later stages.
steps.check: The surface wets evenly: no beading.

chips.t: organics go first because they hide the rest
institution-only chemistry

spec.control: Bath age and temperature, set by the lab
spec.ooc: Beading or stains: the wafer is re-cleaned

steps.deep: A strongly oxidising treatment turns organic residues into gases and leaves a thin chemical oxide behind [@kern1990]. Nothing about the mixture is published here: it is handled only by trained staff under the lab’s own rules.

steps.title: Dissolve the thin oxide
steps.do: A short dip dissolves the thin skin of oxide on top. Metals and particles trapped inside it come away with it, and bare silicon is left.
steps.check: The surface sheds water: bare silicon is hydrophobic.

chips.t: frees what the oxide had trapped
institution-only chemistry

spec.control: Dip time and bath condition, set by the lab
spec.ooc: Water still sheets on the wafer: oxide left behind

steps.deep: The etchant for this stage is among the most dangerous chemicals in a fab. It is institution-only, handled only under supervision, and this manual shows only its result: clean, bare silicon that must move on quickly before it reoxidises.

steps.title: Lift the particles off
steps.do: A gentle bath, often helped by sound waves, undercuts each grain by a whisker of material and charges grains and wafer alike so they push apart.
steps.check: A test wafer shows the particle count fell by the expected share.

chips.t: each pass removes a fixed share of what is left
institution-only chemistry

spec.tool: Wet bench, often with megasonic agitation
spec.ooc: Particles return: the bath or rinse water is dirty

steps.deep: If one pass removes a fraction η, the count after n passes is N₀(1 − η)ⁿ, so a second pass helps far less than the first. The cleaning theatre lets you try it.

steps.title: Pull out metal traces
steps.do: A last bath takes metal atoms such as iron off the surface before any furnace can drive them into the silicon.
steps.check: Lifetime or surface-photovoltage maps on a monitor wafer stay clean.

chips.t: iron shortens the life of every electron
institution-only chemistry

spec.ooc: Short lifetimes on monitors: stop the furnace queue

steps.deep: Interstitial iron is a recombination centre. The electron lifetime falls as τ = 1/(σₙ v_th N_Fe): at 10¹⁰ iron atoms per cm³ it is about 180 µs, at 10¹² about 1.8 µs [@istratov1999] [@macdonald2001]. Image sensors and solar cells notice first.

steps.title: Rinse, dry and count again
steps.do: Rinse in ultrapure water, spin dry, and scan the wafer again. Only a wafer that passes may go into a shared furnace.
steps.check: Particle count below the lab’s limit, and the wafer goes straight to the furnace.

chips.t: ultrapure water between and after every bath [@kern1990]
a dirty wafer contaminates every lot after it

spec.tool: Spin rinser-dryer and laser particle scanner
spec.purpose: Leave a dry, clean, counted wafer
spec.control: Particle count; time from clean to furnace
spec.ooc: Too many particles: clean again before the furnace

steps.deep: Killer particles become the defect density D₀ that the yield model turns into lost dies [@stapper1983]. Kern’s review traces how cleaning methods evolved as the particles that mattered grew smaller [@kern1990].

variant.title: Four kinds of dirt, four kinds of damage
variant.lead: Each stage targets one kind of contamination, and each kind breaks a chip in its own way.

facts.t: The sequence was developed at RCA Laboratories in 1965 and published in 1970
With an inverse-cube size distribution, halving the killer size makes four times as many particles deadly
Iron in silicon is one of the most harmful metal contaminants for carrier lifetime
At 10¹² iron atoms per cm³ the electron lifetime drops to about 1.8 µs

variant.safety: Every cleaning bath in this manual uses chemistry that is handled only inside a cleanroom, by trained people, with the lab’s own procedures and protective equipment. None of it is described here, and none of it should ever be tried elsewhere.

leave_out: No chemistry, concentrations, temperatures or times are given for any bath: they are institution-only.
Particle removal is modelled as a fixed fraction per pass; real removal depends on particle size, material and how long it has been stuck.
Only iron is followed as a metal; copper, nickel and others behave differently.
Drying marks, surface roughening and re-deposition from the rinse are not drawn.

manuals.title: Grow glass on the silicon
manuals.subtitle: Thermal oxidation: load, ramp, oxidise dry or wet, anneal, unload, measure
manuals.route: Every route that starts with silicon: field oxide, gate oxide, masking and screen oxides
manuals.intro: Silicon makes its own insulator. Heat it in oxygen or steam and a layer of silicon dioxide grows from the surface down, part of it made of silicon taken from the wafer itself. That glass is the best-behaved interface any semiconductor has, and it made the planar process and the MOSFET possible.
manuals.model_after: Growth follows the Deal–Grove law [@dealgrove1965] with the rate constants used across the site [@hollauer_dg]; furnace practice follows Plummer, Deal and Griffin [@plummer2000]; the recipes and thicknesses come from a four-mask NMOS run in a university teaching cleanroom [@cleanroom_run_fab2024].

steps.title: Load the boat
steps.do: Stand the wafers in a quartz boat with a monitor wafer at each end and push it slowly into the furnace while it idles under nitrogen.
steps.check: Every slot logged; monitors in place.

chips.t: load straight from cleaning [@plummer2000]
slow push avoids warp and slip

spec.purpose: Get clean wafers into the heat
spec.ooc: Wafers waited too long after cleaning: clean again

steps.deep: A wafer that waits after cleaning collects a native oxide and particles that would be sealed under the new film. Monitor wafers at both ends of the load show whether every position saw the same heat [@plummer2000].

steps.title: Ramp up in nitrogen
steps.do: Raise the furnace to the oxidation temperature under nitrogen, so no oxide grows until the temperature is steady.
steps.check: All zones read the set point.

chips.t: the rate depends exponentially on temperature [@dealgrove1965]

spec.ooc: A zone off its set point: stop and recalibrate

steps.deep: Both Deal–Grove rate constants follow Arrhenius laws, so a few degrees of error changes the thickness measurably [@dealgrove1965] [@hollauer_dg]. Ramp rates and set points are part of every qualified recipe.

steps.title: Grow a gate oxide in dry oxygen
steps.do: Switch the gas to dry oxygen. A thin, dense oxide grows slowly and evenly from the surface down.
steps.check: The monitor wafer will tell; nothing to see yet.

chips.t: teaching run: 1100 °C for 60 minutes gave 114 nm [@cleanroom_run_fab2024]
Deal–Grove predicts 111 nm [@dealgrove1965] [@hollauer_dg]

spec.purpose: Grow the insulator under the gate
spec.control: Time at temperature and gas flow
spec.ooc: Thin or thick on the monitor: check temperature profile and flow

steps.deep: Oxygen diffuses through the oxide already grown and reacts at the silicon below. A thin film grows linearly, at B/A; a thick one slows to x² = Bt [@dealgrove1965]. For every nanometre of oxide, 0.44 nm of silicon is consumed [@plummer2000].

steps.title: Grow a field oxide in steam
steps.do: For thick isolation, run a short dry step, a long step in steam, and a short dry step again. Steam carries far more oxidant through the oxide, so it grows many times faster.
steps.check: The colour of the monitor wafer has changed through several orders of interference.

chips.t: teaching run: dry–wet–dry, 5–90–5 minutes at 1000 °C [@cleanroom_run_fab2024]
teaching run: 548 nm measured, 517 nm by Deal–Grove [@cleanroom_run_fab2024]

spec.tool: Tube furnace with a steam source
spec.ooc: Thin oxide: the steam source may be running weak

steps.deep: The dry steps give a clean interface underneath and a dense skin on top; the wet step does the bulk of the growth. Earlier runs of the same recipe gave 445 and 522 nm [@teaching_process_manual2023], so run-to-run spread is part of the lesson.

steps.title: Anneal in nitrogen
steps.do: Switch back to nitrogen and hold the temperature for a while. The oxide does not grow, but its charge settles.
steps.check: Gas switched; hold time logged.

chips.t: lowers the fixed charge near the interface [@plummer2000]

spec.ooc: High fixed charge on C–V tests: lengthen the anneal

steps.deep: Charge left in the oxide near the interface shifts the threshold voltage of every transistor built on it. In the teaching run that charge pulled the thresholds negative, which the Process Lab works out from the measured values [@cleanroom_run_char2024].

steps.title: Unload and measure
steps.do: Ramp down slowly, pull the boat out, and measure the monitor wafers at several points with an ellipsometer or a reflectometer.
steps.check: Mean and spread inside the limits for the recipe.

chips.t: a colour chart gives a quick first estimate
silicon consumed: 0.44 nm per nm of oxide [@plummer2000]

spec.ooc: Out of limits: the lot is held and the furnace checked

steps.deep: Ellipsometry fits the change in polarisation of reflected light to thickness and refractive index. A gate oxide is also tested electrically: capacitance against voltage gives its thickness, charge and interface quality [@plummer2000].

variant.title: Dry oxygen versus steam
variant.lead: Dry oxide is slow and dense, for gates. Steam is fast, for thick isolation and masks.

facts.t: Grown oxide masks silicon against dopants
Thermal oxide passivates the silicon surface
Deal and Grove’s linear-parabolic law covers both dry and wet growth
Teaching run: the model lands within 6 % of the measured gate and field oxides

leave_out: Deal–Grove underestimates very thin dry oxides, which grow faster at the start than the law predicts.
The steam source is treated as one atmosphere of water vapour; a weak source gives less.
Stress, orientation effects at edges and dopant-enhanced oxidation are not drawn.
Furnace times and temperatures here are one teaching run’s values, not a qualified recipe for any tool.

manuals.title: Make the photomask
manuals.subtitle: Mask making: blank, write, develop, etch the chrome, strip, measure, inspect and repair, mount the pellicle
manuals.route: Every route: each lithography layer needs its own mask
manuals.next: Manual 4A · Print a pattern with light
manuals.intro: Before a wafer can be patterned, the pattern has to exist as a mask: a plate of glass with a thin opaque film where light must be blocked. A mask is written once, checked obsessively and then used to print thousands of wafers. A device can need between 5 and 40 or more of them.
manuals.model_after: The sequence follows public descriptions from two mask makers [@compugraphics_masks] [@elveflow_masks], with mask types and numbers from the Photomask article [@wiki_photomask].

you_need.label: Mask blank: quartz or glass with chrome and resist
The layout file for this layer

steps.title: Start with a blank
steps.do: Take a plate of fused silica (quartz) or soda-lime glass coated with chrome, an anti-reflective layer and resist.
steps.check: No scratches, pinholes or particles on the blank.

chips.t: fused silica (QZ) or soda-lime glass (SL) [@compugraphics_masks]
reticles are typically quartz [@compugraphics_masks]

spec.control: Blank defect map from the supplier
spec.ooc: Defect on blank: reject it

steps.deep: Quartz transmits deep-ultraviolet light and barely expands with heat, so it is used for reticles in steppers and scanners; soda-lime glass is cheaper and serves for copy masks and contact printing [@compugraphics_masks]. Chromium is used because it blocks ultraviolet light well [@wiki_photomask].

steps.title: Write the pattern
steps.do: A laser or electron beam scans the layout into the resist, piece by piece, straight from the design file.
steps.check: The writer logs every field as written.

chips.t: laser writer with a micromirror array, 0.8 µm pixels [@elveflow_masks]
leading-edge masks: electron-beam writers [@levinson2019]

spec.purpose: Turn the layout into a latent image
spec.ooc: Stitching error between fields: rewrite on a new blank

steps.deep: No mask exists yet to copy from, so the pattern is drawn directly. A laser writer flashes frames through a digital micromirror device and stitches them together [@elveflow_masks]. Masks for advanced nodes are written with electron beams [@levinson2019].

steps.title: Develop
steps.do: Dissolve the written resist so the chrome shows through where the pattern must become clear.
steps.check: Openings are clean down to the chrome.

chips.t: developer: institution-only handling

spec.ooc: Scum: rework or reject

steps.deep: This is the same chemistry as wafer lithography (Manual 4A), on a glass plate instead of silicon [@compugraphics_masks].

steps.title: Etch the chrome
steps.do: Remove the chrome through the resist openings so light can pass there.
steps.check: Clear areas are fully transparent.

chips.t: a chemical process that removes chrome selectively [@elveflow_masks]
chrome etchant: institution-only

spec.purpose: Transfer the pattern into the chrome
spec.ooc: Chrome left in openings: re-etch or reject

steps.deep: The chrome etchant is hazardous chemistry handled only by trained staff, so this step is conceptual here. Advanced masks are etched in a plasma instead, for the same reason wafers are: straighter edges [@levinson2019].

steps.title: Strip the resist
steps.do: Remove the remaining resist. What is left is the chrome pattern on glass.
steps.check: No resist residue.

chips.t: chrome on quartz or soda-lime, with the anti-reflective coating [@elveflow_masks]

spec.ooc: Particles: clean again

steps.deep: The plate now works like a stencil: it blocks light where chrome remains and passes it where chrome was etched.

steps.title: Measure the critical dimensions
steps.do: Measure line widths at many points and check them against the design.
steps.check: Every measured width is inside its tolerance.

chips.t: CD measurement [@compugraphics_masks]

spec.purpose: Prove the mask prints the right size
spec.ooc: Out of tolerance: reject the mask

steps.deep: A reticle used at 4× reduction prints features four times smaller than it carries [@wiki_photomask], so a mask error also shrinks by four on the wafer.

steps.title: Inspect and repair
steps.do: Compare the whole mask against the design to find any defect, and repair it if possible.
steps.check: No printable defect remains.

chips.t: inspect, then repair if necessary [@compugraphics_masks]

spec.ooc: Unrepairable defect: rewrite the mask

steps.deep: One defect on a mask repeats on every die it prints, on every wafer. That is why masks are inspected far more strictly than wafers. A small chrome spot (drawn here between the lines) would be removed or patched by repair tools.

steps.title: Mount the pellicle
steps.do: Glue a frame over the pattern with a thin transparent film stretched across it. Dust now lands on the film, out of focus.
steps.check: The pellicle is flat and free of particles.

chips.t: a protective pellicle is attached last [@compugraphics_masks]
pellicle film on a frame glued over one side [@wiki_photomask]

spec.ooc: Particle under the pellicle: remove, clean, remount

steps.deep: A particle sitting on the pellicle is millimetres above the pattern, far outside the depth of focus of the projection lens, so it does not print [@wiki_photomask].

variant.title: From contact masks to EUV reticles
variant.lead: As features shrank, masks changed from simple chrome stencils to precision optical parts.

facts.t: Steppers and scanners project the mask pattern shrunk four or five times
Reduction ratios on offer include 1:1, 2.5:1, 4:1 and 5:1
Features of about 150 nm and below generally need phase-shifting masks
EUV masks reflect light from many alternating molybdenum and silicon layers
One high-end phase-shift mask could cost up to $100,000 in 2006
A functioning device can need between 5 and 40+ masks

leave_out: Optical proximity correction and inverse lithography reshape the drawn features on the mask; they are not drawn here.
Mask writing times, data volumes and write strategies are only mentioned.

manuals.title: Print a pattern with light
manuals.subtitle: Photolithography: prime, coat, bake, align, expose, develop, inspect
manuals.route: Teaching CMOS (i-line or deep-UV stepper), with the EUV variant used at 2 nm-class nodes
manuals.intro: Every layer of a chip starts as a picture. Lithography copies that picture from a mask into a thin light-sensitive film called photoresist. The film then protects some parts of the wafer while the next step (etch or implant) changes the rest. A modern chip goes through this loop dozens of times.
manuals.model_after: The step list follows a public baseline traveler, the UC Berkeley Marvell Nanolab cmos150 run card [@nanolab_cmos150], and the run card of a real four-mask NMOS run in a university teaching cleanroom [@cleanroom_run_fab2024].

steps.title: Prime the surface
steps.do: Expose the wafer to hexamethyldisilazane (HMDS) vapour. It turns the oxide surface water-repellent so the resist sticks.
steps.check: Water beads up on a test wafer instead of spreading.

chips.t: HMDS prime, program 1 on the coat track [@nanolab_cmos150]
teaching run: 10 min dehydration bake at 110 °C, then 5 min of primer vapour [@cleanroom_run_fab2024]

spec.control: Contact angle on a monitor wafer
spec.ooc: Resist lifts during develop: re-clean and re-prime

steps.deep: HMDS caps surface hydroxyl groups with methyl groups, so the surface stops attracting water. HMDS itself is a hazardous chemical and is handled only inside the closed prime oven.

steps.title: Dispense the resist
steps.do: Drop a few millilitres of liquid resist onto the centre of the wafer.
steps.check: One round puddle, no bubbles.

chips.t: a few ml per wafer [@microchem_basics]

spec.ooc: Comets and streaks: filter or degas the resist

steps.deep: Resist can be dispensed onto a still wafer (static) or onto a slowly turning one (dynamic). Air bubbles in the resist take about 20 minutes to escape from thin resists and hours from viscous ones [@microchem_basics].

steps.title: Spin it thin
steps.do: Spin the wafer fast. The resist flings outward and thins to an even film as its solvent evaporates.
steps.check: An even colour across the wafer. A thicker ring at the edge (the edge bead) is normal and is removed.

chips.t: 2000–4000 rpm for 20–30 s [@microchem_basics]
Berkeley baseline: 4500 Å of UV-210 [@nanolab_cmos150]
teaching run: 3000 rpm for 30 s [@cleanroom_run_fab2024]

spec.control: Film thickness by reflectometry; uniformity map
spec.ooc: Too thick: raise spin speed. Doubling the speed thins the film about 1.4×

steps.deep: Thickness falls roughly as one over the square root of spin speed, so t ∝ 1/√ω and doubling the speed thins the film by about 1.4× [@microchem_basics]. Thinning stops once enough solvent has evaporated that the film no longer flows. After spinning, about 10 % (thin resists) to 35 % (thick resists) of the film is still solvent [@microchem_basics].

steps.title: Soft bake
steps.do: Bake the wafer briefly on a hotplate to drive out most of the remaining solvent.
steps.check: The film is dry and no longer tacky.

chips.t: solvent falls to about 3–5 % [@microchem_basics]
teaching run: 90 °C for 90 s on a hotplate [@cleanroom_run_fab2024]

spec.control: Hotplate temperature log; thickness after bake
spec.ooc: Under-baked film smears and dissolves too fast in develop

steps.deep: The soft bake is also called the post-apply bake (PAB) [@willson_flow]. Too little bake leaves solvent that speeds dissolution everywhere; too much starts to destroy the light-sensitive compound.

steps.title: Align the mask
steps.do: Load the photomask, a glass plate with a chrome pattern, and line its marks up with the marks the last layer left on the wafer.
steps.check: The alignment marks overlap within the tool’s overlay limit.

chips.t: chrome mask, one per layer [@nanolab_cmos150]
pre-alignment on [@nanolab_cmos150]
teaching run, manual aligner: 0.2–1.4 µm overlay error [@cleanroom_run_fab2024]

spec.purpose: Register this layer to the last
spec.ooc: Overlay out of limit: rework (strip resist and repeat from step 1)

steps.deep: Each layer must land on top of the last. The error between them is called overlay, and it is measured on dedicated marks after develop. A failed layer is reworked: the resist is stripped and the module runs again, because nothing has yet changed the wafer underneath.

steps.title: Expose
steps.do: Flash ultraviolet light through the mask. Where light lands, the resist changes chemistry and will later wash away.
steps.check: The tool reports the planned dose and focus for every field.

chips.t: dose 30 mJ/cm² in the Berkeley baseline [@nanolab_cmos150]
smallest pitch λ / (2·NA) [@mack2007]
teaching run: i-line contact exposure, 9 s [@cleanroom_run_fab2024]

spec.tool: Stepper or scanner (i-line, KrF, ArF, ArF immersion, EUV)
spec.control: Dose and focus per field; focus-exposure matrix on monitors
spec.ooc: Lines too wide or narrow: adjust dose. Lines fade at the wafer edge: check focus and flatness

steps.deep: The lens can only collect so many of the diffraction orders that a fine pattern sends out. With tilted (off-axis) light the smallest printable pitch is λ / (2·NA), which is k₁ = 0.25 in the Rayleigh form [@mack2007]. The Physics Lab’s aerial-image simulator computes this image live.

steps.title: Post-exposure bake
steps.do: Bake again. In chemically amplified resist the light made a little acid, and the heat lets each acid molecule change many more.
steps.check: Bake time and temperature match the resist’s sheet.

chips.t: “chemical amplification” [@willson_flow]
post-exposure bake, program 1 [@nanolab_cmos150]

spec.control: Hotplate uniformity; delay between expose and bake
spec.ooc: Line width drifts with bake temperature: requalify the hotplate

steps.deep: One photon makes one acid molecule. During the post-exposure bake (PEB) that acid acts as a catalyst and changes many polymer groups, so the image is ‘amplified’ [@willson_flow]. Acid also diffuses during the bake, which blurs the edge a little: one source of line-edge roughness.

steps.title: Develop
steps.do: Flood the wafer with developer. The exposed resist dissolves and the oxide shows through the openings.
steps.check: Openings are clear down to the oxide, with no scum.

chips.t: exposed areas dissolve quickly [@willson_flow]
aqueous alkaline developer: institution-only handling
teaching run: 60 s [@cleanroom_run_fab2024]

spec.purpose: Turn the latent image into openings
spec.control: After-develop inspection; CD on test structures
spec.ooc: Scum in openings: descum in a short oxygen plasma, or rework

steps.deep: In a positive resist the exposed regions become very soluble and are removed quickly [@willson_flow]. Developer chemistry is handled inside the track by trained staff; this manual describes it only conceptually.

steps.title: Inspect and measure
steps.do: Look at the pattern under a microscope, then measure line width and overlay.
steps.check: Critical dimension (CD) and overlay are inside their limits. If not, strip and redo the module.

chips.t: CD-SEM (critical-dimension scanning electron microscope)
overlay metrology

spec.ooc: Rework: strip and repeat from step 1

steps.deep: This is the last moment a mistake is cheap. After etch or implant the wafer itself has changed and cannot be reworked.

steps.title: Hard bake
steps.do: Bake the patterned resist in an oven so it is tough enough to survive the etch or implant that comes next.
steps.check: Resist edges stay sharp, not rounded.

chips.t: more than 30 min at 120 °C in the oven [@nanolab_cmos150]

spec.purpose: Harden resist for etch or implant
spec.ooc: Resist flows and rounds: bake was too hot

steps.deep: The Berkeley run card also lists a descum step here, skipped when no tool for the wafer size was available [@nanolab_cmos150]. Next the wafer goes to Manual 5, Etch, where the resist protects the oxide under it.

variant.title: Variant: extreme ultraviolet (EUV) at 2 nm-class nodes
variant.lead: EUV light is absorbed by glass and even by air, so an EUV scanner works in vacuum and uses mirrors instead of lenses. The mask is a mirror too.

facts.t: Wavelength 13.5 nm
Light is made when a CO₂ laser hits a falling tin droplet with two pulses, up to 50,000 times a second
Multilayer mirrors, typically 40 Mo/Si bilayers, reflect up to 70 %
The optics shrink the mask pattern 4× onto the wafer
NXE: NA 0.33, 13 nm resolution. EXE (High-NA): NA 0.55, 8 nm resolution
So few photons land per feature that random ‘stochastic’ defects appear: missing or bridged lines

variant.safety: The tin plasma source uses a high-power industrial laser inside a sealed machine. It is described here only to explain how the tool works.

leave_out: Real recipes depend on the exact resist, film stack and tool. The ranges here are teaching ranges from public sources, not a qualified recipe.
Reflections from the layers under the resist (standing waves) and anti-reflective coatings are not drawn.
Optical proximity correction (OPC), source-mask optimisation and multiple patterning are covered in the lithography chapter, not in this module.
Developer and primer chemistry are named but never given as concentrations or procedures.

manuals.title: Carve the pattern into the film
manuals.subtitle: Plasma (reactive ion) etch: load, pump down, flow gas, strike plasma, etch, endpoint, over-etch, strip, measure
manuals.route: Teaching CMOS and modern logic: every layer that lithography patterns is etched next
manuals.next: Manual 6A · Diffusion, Manual 6B · Implantation, Manual 7A · Metal or Manual 7B · Deposition
manuals.intro: Lithography only draws the pattern in resist. Etching copies it into the film underneath: oxide, polysilicon, nitride or metal. A wet etch dissolves the film in liquid and eats sideways as fast as down. A plasma etch fires ions straight down, so the walls stay vertical and small features survive.
manuals.model_after: Tool facts come from public university cleanroom pages [@byu_rie] [@ucsb_rie1]. The wet-versus-dry comparison uses measured widths from a four-mask NMOS run in a university teaching cleanroom [@cleanroom_run_fab2024].

steps.title: Load the patterned wafer
steps.do: Place the wafer on the lower electrode of the etcher. The hard-baked resist covers everything that must stay.
steps.check: Resist edges are sharp and the openings are clean.

chips.t: parallel-plate RIE, 13.56 MHz [@byu_rie]

spec.tool: Reactive ion etcher, load lock or open chamber
spec.purpose: Bring the patterned wafer to the electrode
spec.control: Wafer seated flat; correct recipe selected
spec.ooc: Wafer chipped or off-centre: unload and inspect

steps.deep: In a parallel-plate reactive ion etcher the wafer sits on the powered electrode. The BYU tool is an Anelva DEM-451 with a 14-inch cathode [@byu_rie].

steps.title: Pump down
steps.do: Close the chamber and pump the air out until the pressure is very low.
steps.check: The gauge reads the base pressure before any gas flows.

chips.t: pump to 20 mTorr or less first [@byu_rie]
ultimate pressure mid 10⁻⁷ Torr on a turbo-pumped tool [@ucsb_rie1]

spec.purpose: Remove air and water before the process gas
spec.ooc: Will not pump down: check the door seal, then call staff

steps.deep: Air and water vapour would react in the plasma and change the etch. Pumping first also makes the gas mixture repeatable from run to run. The tool’s guide warns never to switch on the RF power while the chamber is at high pressure [@byu_rie].

steps.title: Flow the process gas
steps.do: Let a measured flow of etch gas into the chamber. Fluorine-based gases etch silicon, oxide and nitride.
steps.check: Flows and pressure settle at the recipe values.

chips.t: CF₄ with O₂ for Si, Si₃N₄ and SiO₂ [@byu_rie]
gas supply is institution-only

spec.ooc: Flow will not stabilise: abort the run and call staff

steps.deep: The gas is chosen for the film: fluorine chemistries for silicon and its oxide and nitride [@byu_rie], chlorine for aluminium and compound semiconductors [@ucsb_rie1]. Gas cylinders, cabinets and exhaust scrubbing are run by trained staff, so this manual names the gases but gives no handling procedure.

steps.title: Strike the plasma
steps.do: Switch on the radio-frequency power. The gas glows: it has become a plasma of ions and reactive fragments.
steps.check: A steady glow, and reflected power stays small.

chips.t: 13.56 MHz at a few hundred watts [@wiki_rie]
pressure rises 20–40 mTorr when RF turns on [@byu_rie]
reflected power 1–10 W [@byu_rie]

params.name: Operating pressure
params.value: a few mTorr to a few hundred mTorr

spec.control: Forward and reflected power; glow colour
spec.ooc: Reflected power high: retune the match or stop

steps.deep: Electrons pick up energy from the RF field and break gas molecules into ions and radicals. Light electrons charge the wafer electrode negative, a DC self-bias of typically a few hundred volts [@wiki_rie]. The RF supply is high voltage, so the chamber is interlocked.

steps.title: Etch straight down
steps.do: Ions accelerate across the sheath and strike the wafer head-on. Where the resist is open the film is etched downward, and the walls stay vertical.
steps.check: The film thins only in the openings.

chips.t: anisotropic unless run in a high-pressure, purely chemical mode [@byu_rie]
example: GaAs at 2 mTorr Cl₂, 350 V bias, about 200 nm/min [@ucsb_rie1]

spec.purpose: Transfer the pattern into the film
spec.control: Etch time against the measured rate on a monitor
spec.ooc: Sloped walls: lower the pressure so ions dominate

steps.deep: Ion bombardment speeds the chemical reaction only on surfaces the ions hit, the floor of each opening, so the etch is anisotropic [@wiki_rie]. Narrow openings etch more slowly than wide ones, because fewer reactive molecules find their way down a deep, narrow hole [@coburn1989]. The Fab Journey’s etch theatre simulates this lag.

steps.title: Stop at the layer below
steps.do: Watch for the moment the film clears and the layer underneath shows. That is the endpoint.
steps.check: Every opening is clear down to the silicon.

chips.t: selectivity: film rate ÷ stop-layer rate
CF₄/O₂ rate falls from Si to Si₃N₄ to SiO₂ [@byu_rie]

spec.tool: Reactive ion etcher with endpoint detection
spec.control: Endpoint signal or timed etch from monitor wafers
spec.ooc: Etched into the silicon: lower power, or choose a more selective chemistry

steps.deep: Selectivity is the ratio of etch rates of the film and the layer that must survive. In a plain CF₄/O₂ plasma silicon etches faster than nitride, and nitride faster than oxide [@byu_rie], so when oxide is etched down to silicon the silicon is the faster one: keep the over-etch short. Production oxide etches use other fluorocarbon chemistries to protect the silicon.

steps.title: Over-etch a little
steps.do: Keep etching for a short extra time so thin spots and slow, narrow openings clear too.
steps.check: No film is left in any opening, even small ones.

chips.t: strong loading effect: more open area etches slower [@byu_rie]

spec.control: Over-etch as a percentage of the main etch
spec.ooc: Resist eroded through: thicker resist or a hard mask

steps.deep: The etch rate depends on how much of the wafer is open, the loading effect [@byu_rie], and on how narrow each opening is [@coburn1989]. Over-etch covers both. It also erodes the resist, which is why deep etches use a hard mask of oxide or nitride instead.

steps.title: Strip the resist
steps.do: Burn the leftover resist off in an oxygen plasma, then clean the wafer.
steps.check: No resist residue under the microscope.

chips.t: oxygen plasma ashing [@plummer2000]

spec.ooc: Residue left: ash again

steps.deep: An oxygen plasma turns the organic resist into carbon dioxide and water vapour [@plummer2000]. Wet strippers are also used, but they are institution-only chemistry.

steps.title: Measure the result
steps.do: Measure the etched lines and compare them with the drawn widths and with the resist before etch.
steps.check: Etch bias (etched width minus resist width) is inside its limit.

chips.t: teaching run, wet oxide etch: openings grew 2.48 µm on average [@cleanroom_run_fab2024]

spec.ooc: Bias too large: shorten the etch or switch from wet to dry

steps.deep: A wet etch undercuts the resist by about the film thickness on each side, plus any over-etch. In the teaching run the openings in the field oxide came out 2.48 µm wider on average than the resist openings [@cleanroom_run_fab2024]. A plasma etch keeps that bias near zero, which is what makes nanometre features possible.

variant.title: Wet etch versus plasma etch
variant.lead: Both remove film through the resist openings. The difference is direction: a liquid etches in every direction, a plasma etches mostly down.

facts.t: Wet chemical etching gives typically isotropic profiles; RIE gives very anisotropic ones
Teaching run: wet-etched oxide openings came out 2.48 µm wider than the resist on average
Teaching run: polysilicon gates came out 1.34 µm narrower after their wet etch
Inductively coupled plasma (ICP) sources reach very high plasma densities; a separate RF bias on the wafer then sets the ion energy
Deep reactive ion etching (the Bosch process) alternates etch and passivation to cut deep vertical trenches
Narrow openings etch slower than wide ones (aspect-ratio-dependent etching)

variant.safety: Wet etchants for oxide (hydrofluoric acid and buffered oxide etch) and for polysilicon are among the most dangerous chemicals in a cleanroom. They are named here only to explain the comparison. No concentrations or procedures are given.

tables.title: Which etch for which job
head: Wet etch
Plasma (RIE)
rows: +2.48 µm on oxide openings in a teaching run [@cleanroom_run_fab2024]
every critical layer in modern chips

leave_out: Etch rates depend on the exact tool, gas mix, power and loading; the numbers here are examples from public tool pages, not a qualified recipe.
Polymer build-up on sidewalls, plasma damage and charging are not drawn.
Atomic layer etching and high-aspect-ratio memory etches are only mentioned.
Gas handling and wet chemistry are named but never given as procedures.

manuals.title: Bake the dopant into the silicon
manuals.subtitle: Furnace diffusion: open windows, predeposit, remove the source, drive in, measure
manuals.route: Teaching CMOS (source and drain) and the historical planar process
manuals.intro: Before ion implanters, every junction was made in a furnace, and teaching cleanrooms still make them that way. A dopant-rich source sits on bare silicon, atoms soak in from the surface, the source is removed and a second bake drives them deeper. Oxide decides where the dopant can go. The dopant sources are institution-only, so those stages stay conceptual.
manuals.model_after: Profiles follow the textbook predeposition and drive-in solutions [@plummer2000] with intrinsic diffusivities [@uiuc_diffusivity]; oxide masking follows Frosch and Derick [@frosch1957]; run values come from a four-mask NMOS run in a university teaching cleanroom [@cleanroom_run_fab2024] [@cleanroom_run_char2024].

you_need.label: Wafer with windows opened in the oxide

steps.title: Check the windows are open
steps.do: Look at the wafer under the microscope. Where the oxide has been etched away, bare silicon shows; everywhere else oxide will block the dopant.
steps.check: Windows are clean and fully open; no oxide film left in them.

chips.t: oxide masks dopant diffusion [@frosch1957]
in MOS the gate masks the channel

spec.ooc: Film left in the window: the junction comes out uneven

steps.deep: Dopants diffuse far more slowly in silicon dioxide than in silicon, so an oxide layer masks the silicon beneath it [@frosch1957]. Hoerni’s planar process made every junction this way, through windows in the oxide [@hoerni1962].

steps.title: Coat the dopant source
steps.do: A thin film rich in dopant is put on the wafer by trained staff. It touches the silicon only where the windows are open.
steps.check: The film covers the wafer evenly.

chips.t: the source keeps the surface concentration fixed
dopant sources are institution-only

spec.tool: Coater or source boat, staff only
spec.ooc: Uneven film: the lab strips and recoats

steps.deep: The source can be a spun-on film, a solid source wafer or a dopant gas; all hold the silicon surface at a high, fixed concentration while the furnace runs [@plummer2000]. Every source chemistry is institution-only, and some are highly toxic.

steps.title: Predeposit in the furnace
steps.do: In the hot furnace dopant atoms hop from the film into the open silicon. The silicon near the surface fills up first.
steps.check: A control wafer travels with the batch.

chips.t: the surface stays pinned at the source’s concentration
the dose grows only as the square root of time

spec.tool: Horizontal tube furnace with the source, staff only
spec.control: Set by the lab; control wafer measured afterwards
spec.ooc: Control wafer out of range: the lab decides on a rerun

steps.deep: With the surface pinned at Cs the profile is a complementary error function, and the dose grows as √t: double the time and only 41 % more dopant goes in [@plummer2000]. The furnace step with a dopant source is institution-only.

steps.title: Remove the source
steps.do: The spent film is removed, so the amount of dopant in the silicon is now fixed.
steps.check: The control wafer’s sheet resistance confirms dopant went in.

chips.t: from here the dose cannot change
institution-only chemistry

spec.ooc: Residue left: re-clean before the drive-in

steps.deep: Removing the film is a wet chemical step and stays institution-only [@plummer2000]. Teaching labs keep a second control wafer so a weak predeposition can be repeated.

steps.title: Drive in and grow oxide
steps.do: A second, longer bake without any source spreads the same dopant deeper. The same bake grows an oxide over everything.
steps.check: Oxide on the bare control wafer has the target thickness.

chips.t: teaching run: 1050 °C for 37 minutes [@cleanroom_run_fab2024]
teaching run: 62.9 nm of oxide on the control [@cleanroom_run_fab2024]
junction creeps sideways about 80 % of its depth [@plummer2000]

spec.purpose: Push the junction deeper and insulate the top
spec.ooc: Oxide off target: check the furnace profile and the clean before it

steps.deep: With a fixed dose the profile relaxes into a half-Gaussian, and Dt adds up over both bakes [@plummer2000]. The Virtual Fab follows this run’s drive-in and puts its computed oxide, 62.0 nm, beside the measured 62.9 nm.

steps.title: Measure the sheet resistance
steps.do: Touch four needles in a line to a diffused test resistor or the control wafer. Push current through the outer two and read the voltage across the inner two.
steps.check: The sheet resistance is in the expected range.

chips.t: teaching run: 57.1 Ω across a 201 µm × 11 µm resistor [@cleanroom_run_char2024]
that is about 3.1 Ω per square [@cleanroom_run_char2024]

spec.purpose: Check the doped layer conducts as designed
spec.control: Sheet resistance on control wafers and test resistors
spec.ooc: Too high: too little dose or too shallow; check the predeposition

steps.deep: R_s = R·W/L. The four-point probe needs no correction for contact resistance because the voltage pins carry no current [@plummer2000]. The site’s intrinsic-diffusivity model gives about ten times this value: heavy phosphorus diffuses faster than the intrinsic rate [@uiuc_diffusivity].

variant.title: Furnace diffusion versus ion implantation
variant.lead: Both put dopant into the silicon. A furnace soaks it in from the surface; an implanter fires a counted dose to a chosen depth.

facts.t: Oxide masks dopant diffusion, the discovery that made planar windows possible
Hoerni’s planar process formed junctions by diffusion through oxide windows
Ion implantation took over most doping steps from the 1970s
Teaching run: a diffused resistor measured about 3.1 Ω per square

variant.safety: Dopant sources, whether spun-on films, solid sources or gases, are institution-only. So is stripping the source. This manual gives only what each stage does and what was measured afterwards.

leave_out: Diffusivity is the intrinsic value; heavy doping, oxidation and point defects speed real diffusion up, so real junctions are deeper.
The predeposition time and surface concentration of the teaching run were not recorded.
Dopant segregation into the growing oxide is ignored.
No source chemistry or furnace procedure is given: those stages are institution-only.

manuals.title: Fire dopant atoms into the silicon
manuals.subtitle: Ion implantation: mask, tilt, implant, see the damage, anneal, measure
manuals.route: Modern logic and most teaching CMOS flows: wells, thresholds, sources and drains
manuals.intro: An implanter turns dopant atoms into ions, speeds them up through a voltage and fires them into the wafer. The voltage sets how deep they go and a meter counts every one, so the dose and depth are far more precise than any furnace diffusion. The ion source uses institution-only gases, so that part stays conceptual.
manuals.model_after: Ranges follow the stopping-power model of the site’s implant simulator, checked against published examples [@tuttle_implant]; implanter practice and annealing follow Plummer, Deal and Griffin [@plummer2000]; Dennard’s scaled MOSFET shows why implantation took over [@dennard1974].

you_need.label: Anneal furnace or rapid thermal processor

steps.title: Check the mask is thick enough
steps.do: Measure the resist. It must stop every ion where the silicon should stay undoped, and its edges decide where the doped region starts.
steps.check: Resist thickness is well above the ion range for the planned energy.

chips.t: gates and spacers mask too: self-alignment [@plummer2000]

spec.purpose: Make sure the mask will stop the ions
spec.ooc: Resist too thin: ions punch through; recoat

steps.deep: High-energy implants need microns of resist. In a self-aligned MOS process the polysilicon gate itself masks the channel, so source and drain land exactly beside it [@plummer2000].

steps.title: Make the ion beam
steps.do: Trained staff run the ion source, which ionises a dopant-bearing feed. A magnet then picks out only the ions of the right mass.
steps.check: The beam current is steady on the right mass.

chips.t: feed gases are institution-only
the analysing magnet sorts ions by mass

spec.tool: Ion source and analysing magnet, staff only
spec.purpose: Make a pure beam of one dopant
spec.ooc: Wrong mass peak: the lab retunes the magnet

steps.deep: Many dopant feed gases are highly toxic and are handled only inside the tool by trained staff [@plummer2000]. Nothing about them is given here.

steps.title: Implant at a tilt
steps.do: Accelerate the ions and scan the beam across the tilted wafer until the meter has counted the full dose.
steps.check: The integrated dose matches the recipe.

chips.t: energy sets depth: phosphorus at 100 keV stops near 0.12 µm [@tuttle_implant]
boron at 80 keV stops near 0.24 µm [@tuttle_implant]
a few degrees of tilt stops channelling [@plummer2000]

spec.purpose: Put a counted dose at a chosen depth
spec.control: Beam current integrated over time; scan uniformity
spec.ooc: Dose off: the run is held and the Faraday cup checked

steps.deep: Each ion loses energy to nuclei and to electrons until it stops. The stopping depths form a near-Gaussian with projected range Rp and straggle ΔRp; the dose is the beam charge divided by the ion charge and the area [@plummer2000].

steps.title: See the damage
steps.do: Look at what the ions left behind: every one displaced many silicon atoms, and a heavy dose leaves the top layer amorphous. Most dopant is not yet active.
steps.check: A damage or sheet-resistance check on a monitor wafer.

chips.t: one ion displaces hundreds of atoms [@plummer2000]

spec.purpose: Know the state before the anneal
spec.ooc: Unexpected damage level: check dose and beam heating

steps.deep: Implanted atoms sit mostly between lattice sites at first. Pre-amorphising implants are sometimes used on purpose so the crystal regrows cleanly from the undamaged silicon below [@plummer2000].

steps.title: Strip the resist and anneal
steps.do: Remove the resist, then heat the wafer briefly. The crystal repairs itself and the dopant moves onto lattice sites, where it conducts.
steps.check: Sheet resistance falls to its target.

chips.t: spike and millisecond anneals activate with little diffusion [@plummer2000]

spec.purpose: Activate the dopant and heal the crystal
spec.ooc: Sheet resistance high: too little activation; junction deep: too much heat

steps.deep: Annealing also lets the dopant diffuse, widening the profile by about √(2Dt). Keeping junctions shallow while activating fully is one of the hardest trade-offs in a short-channel transistor [@plummer2000].

steps.title: Measure the result
steps.do: Map the sheet resistance across a monitor wafer with a four-point probe. Less often, a lab sputters a crater and counts the dopant depth by depth.
steps.check: Sheet resistance mean and spread within limits.

chips.t: sheet resistance catches dose errors within minutes [@plummer2000]

spec.ooc: Non-uniform map: check the beam scan

steps.deep: Secondary-ion mass spectrometry gives the real profile, including the channelling tail and the diffusion during the anneal, against which the simulator’s Gaussian can be checked [@plummer2000].

variant.title: From furnace diffusion to ion implantation
variant.lead: Implantation sets dose and depth separately and precisely, which scaled transistors needed.

facts.t: Dennard’s 1974 scaled MOSFET was designed around ion-implanted doping
Implanted channel and source/drain doping replaced furnace diffusion in MOS during the 1970s
Phosphorus at 100 keV stops near 0.12 µm in silicon
Boron at 80 keV stops near 0.24 µm

variant.safety: Implanter ion sources use dopant feed gases that are institution-only, and implanters work at high voltage. Only trained staff run them.

leave_out: The profile is a Gaussian; real profiles are skewed and have a channelling tail.
Damage, amorphisation and transient enhanced diffusion during the anneal are described, not modelled here.
No feed gas, source setting or implanter procedure is given: those are institution-only.
Lateral straggle under the mask edge is taken equal to the vertical straggle.

manuals.title: Wire it up with aluminium
manuals.subtitle: Metallization in a teaching process: open contacts, evaporate aluminium, measure, pattern, etch, sinter
manuals.route: Teaching CMOS and the historical planar process (modern chips use copper: see the damascene theatre)
manuals.intro: Transistors are useless until they are wired together. In the planar era and in teaching cleanrooms today, a film of aluminium covers the whole wafer, touches the silicon through contact holes and is then etched into wires and pads. A low-temperature bake makes each contact conduct well.
manuals.model_after: The sequence and measurements follow a four-mask NMOS run in a university teaching cleanroom [@cleanroom_run_fab2024] and its process manual [@teaching_process_manual2023]; deposition basics follow Plummer, Deal and Griffin [@plummer2000]; the film thickness uses the bulk resistivity of aluminium [@gall2016].

steps.title: Check the contact holes
steps.do: Under the microscope, look into each contact hole. The oxide must be gone right down to the doped silicon, or the metal will not touch it.
steps.check: Every hole is open to silicon; widths are recorded.

chips.t: teaching run: contact holes came out 2.39 µm wider than drawn [@cleanroom_run_fab2024]

spec.control: Hole width; colour of the hole floor
spec.ooc: Oxide left in a hole: an open contact, so etch again

steps.deep: The wet contact etch undercuts the resist, so holes grow; in the teaching run agitation in the bath made the contacts the widest features of all [@cleanroom_run_fab2024].

steps.title: Load and pump down
steps.do: Mount the wafers face down above the source in the evaporator and pump the chamber to high vacuum.
steps.check: The pressure gauge reaches the lab’s base pressure.

chips.t: vacuum lets atoms fly straight to the wafer [@plummer2000]

spec.purpose: Clear the path for the metal atoms
spec.ooc: Pressure will not fall: look for a leak or a dirty chamber

steps.deep: At high vacuum an evaporated atom travels further than the chamber is wide before it hits a gas molecule, so it lands in a straight line from the source [@plummer2000]. That is also why evaporation covers steep steps poorly.

steps.title: Evaporate the aluminium
steps.do: Heat the source until aluminium evaporates. A thin, even film condenses over the whole wafer and into every contact hole.
steps.check: The thickness monitor reaches its target; the film is mirror-bright.

chips.t: aluminium heated in a tungsten boat in vacuum [@cleanroom_run_fab2024]
the film covers the whole wafer [@teaching_process_manual2023]

spec.tool: Thermal evaporator with a resistance-heated boat
spec.ooc: Hazy film: the vacuum or the source was dirty

steps.deep: Evaporation is the oldest way to lay down metal; sputtering, which knocks atoms off a target with ions, replaced it in industry because it covers steps better and handles alloys [@plummer2000]. Noyce’s 1959 patent already ran evaporated aluminium leads over the oxide [@noyce_patent].

steps.title: Measure the film
steps.do: Put a four-point probe on the blanket aluminium and read its sheet resistance.
steps.check: Sheet resistance in the expected range.

chips.t: teaching run: 0.1229 Ω per square [@cleanroom_run_fab2024]
bulk aluminium: 2.65 µΩ·cm [@gall2016]

spec.ooc: Too high: a thin film; check the source charge and the monitor

steps.deep: Thickness follows from t = ρ/R_s. With the bulk value of 2.65 µΩ·cm [@gall2016] the run’s 0.1229 Ω/sq [@cleanroom_run_fab2024] means about 216 nm of aluminium; thin films conduct a little worse than bulk, so the real film is probably slightly thicker.

steps.title: Pattern the wires
steps.do: Coat, expose and develop resist with the metal mask, exactly as in Manual 4A. Resist now covers the wires and pads you want to keep.
steps.check: Resist lines line up with the contacts underneath.

chips.t: the fourth and last mask of the teaching process [@cleanroom_run_fab2024]

spec.ooc: Misaligned: strip the resist and repeat

steps.deep: Overlay matters more here than anywhere: a wire shifted off its contact leaves a transistor unconnected. The teaching run measured its earlier layer-to-layer shifts at up to 1.4 µm [@cleanroom_run_fab2024].

steps.title: Etch the aluminium
steps.do: Exposed aluminium is etched away by trained staff, leaving wires and pads under the resist. The resist is then removed.
steps.check: Wires are separate: no metal bridges between neighbours.

chips.t: lines come out a little narrower than drawn
institution-only chemistry

spec.ooc: Bridges between lines: more etch; missing lines: less

steps.deep: A wet aluminium etch undercuts the resist like every wet etch. In the teaching run the metal lines came out 0.88 µm narrower than drawn on average [@cleanroom_run_fab2024]. Industry etches aluminium in a plasma instead, so the walls stay vertical [@plummer2000].

steps.title: Sinter the contacts
steps.do: Bake the wafer gently so the aluminium and silicon bond at every contact and the contact resistance falls.
steps.check: Contacts behave like resistors, not diodes, on a test structure.

chips.t: teaching run: 400 °C for 20 minutes [@cleanroom_run_fab2024]

spec.ooc: Contacts rectify: sinter longer; junctions short: the sinter ran too hot

steps.deep: Aluminium and silicon dissolve into each other a little at the interface, breaking through any thin oxide left in the hole [@plummer2000]. Too much and the aluminium spikes down through a shallow junction, which is why later processes added barrier layers.

variant.title: From evaporated aluminium to copper damascene
variant.lead: Aluminium wired chips for almost forty years. Copper conducts better but cannot be etched easily, so it is laid into trenches instead.

facts.t: Noyce’s patent, filed in 1959, ran aluminium leads over the oxide to the junctions
Teaching run: evaporated aluminium measured 0.1229 Ω per square
IBM announced full copper wiring in production CMOS in 1997
Bulk copper resists less than bulk aluminium: 1.68 against 2.65 µΩ·cm

variant.safety: The aluminium etch is a wet chemical step and is institution-only. Evaporators use high voltage and high vacuum and are run only by trained users.

leave_out: Step coverage over the contact edges is drawn as perfect; evaporation from a small source thins the film on steep walls.
Thin-film resistivity is taken as the bulk value, so the film thickness is a slight underestimate.
Junction spiking, hillocks and electromigration are mentioned but not modelled here.
No etch chemistry is given: it is institution-only.

manuals.title: Coat every surface evenly
manuals.subtitle: Thin-film deposition: chemical vapour deposition (CVD) and atomic layer deposition (ALD)
manuals.route: Modern logic: liners, spacers, gate dielectrics and the insulators between wiring layers
manuals.next: Manual 8 · Planarization, or Manual 10 · Damascene copper
manuals.intro: Not every film can be grown from the silicon itself. Chemical vapour deposition (CVD) lets gas molecules react on the hot wafer and leave a solid film behind. Atomic layer deposition (ALD) does the same one molecular layer at a time, so the film covers the floor and walls of a deep trench almost as thickly as the top. The precursor gases are institution-only, so those parts stay conceptual.
manuals.model_after: Step coverage follows the trench model in the Fab Journey’s deposition theatre, built on the CVD treatment in Plummer, Deal and Griffin [@plummer2000]; ALD growth per cycle and self-limiting chemistry follow George’s review [@george2010]; the high-k gate dielectric follows Intel’s 45 nm process [@mistry2007].

you_need.label: CVD or ALD chamber (staff-run gas supply)

steps.title: Load and pump down
steps.do: Place the wafer in the chamber through a load lock and pump it down to low pressure, then bring it to the deposition temperature.
steps.check: Base pressure and wafer temperature are at the recipe values.

chips.t: cluster tools pass wafers between chambers without air [@plummer2000]

spec.tool: CVD or ALD chamber with load lock
spec.purpose: Start from a clean, heated, evacuated wafer
spec.control: Base pressure, leak-up rate, wafer temperature
spec.ooc: Leak-up too fast: the chamber is checked before any wafer runs

steps.deep: At low pressure molecules travel in straight lines between wall hits rather than colliding with each other. That is what lets them reach the bottom of a trench, and it is the regime the deposition theatre assumes [@plummer2000].

steps.title: Let in the precursors
steps.do: Trained staff run the gas cabinet. The tool meters a precursor vapour into the chamber, where it meets the hot wafer.
steps.check: Flows are steady at the recipe values set by the lab.

chips.t: precursor gases are institution-only
the tool, not the user, handles every gas line

spec.tool: Gas cabinet and mass-flow controllers, staff only
spec.purpose: Bring the reacting molecules to the wafer
spec.ooc: Flow alarm: the tool stops and staff check the line

steps.deep: Many CVD and ALD precursors are toxic, flammable or ignite in air, so they are stored in ventilated cabinets with leak detection and handled only by trained staff [@plummer2000]. Nothing about their chemistry or settings is given here.

steps.title: Grow the film by CVD
steps.do: Let the precursor react on the hot surfaces. The film grows on the top, the walls and the floor of every trench at once, fastest where the gas arrives first.
steps.check: Thickness on a monitor wafer matches the target.

chips.t: a molecule that reacts on its first hit coats only the mouth [@plummer2000]
a low sticking probability lets molecules bounce down to the floor [@plummer2000]

spec.purpose: Cover the wafer with an insulator or liner
spec.control: Deposition time against rate on monitors; temperature and pressure
spec.ooc: Floor too thin: lower the sticking probability or use ALD

steps.deep: Inside a trench of width w, the gas concentration n falls with depth because every wall hit can consume it. The balance n″ = (3s/2w²)·n makes the film thin out over a depth of about w/√s, where s is the sticking probability. The Fab Journey’s deposition theatre solves that balance as the trench narrows.

steps.title: Grow it one layer at a time (ALD)
steps.do: Pulse the first precursor until it has covered every surface, purge, pulse the second to react with that layer, purge again. Each cycle adds one thin layer everywhere, top to floor.
steps.check: Growth per cycle on a monitor wafer is at its expected value.

chips.t: each half-reaction stops by itself once the surface is covered [@george2010]
aluminium oxide grows about 0.1 nm per cycle [@george2010]

spec.purpose: Make a film of exact thickness that follows every surface
spec.control: Cycle count; pulse and purge times long enough to saturate
spec.ooc: Growth per cycle too high: purges too short, so the gases met and did CVD

steps.deep: Because each half-cycle saturates, ALD does not depend on how much gas reaches each spot, only on whether enough does. That self-limiting step makes it conformal in deep trenches and precise to a fraction of a nanometre, at the price of being slow [@george2010].

steps.title: Build a high-k gate dielectric
steps.do: On a gate stack, use ALD to lay down a hafnium-based insulator a few nanometres thick, then cap it with the gate metal.
steps.check: Thickness and capacitance on monitors are on target.

chips.t: high-k metal gates entered volume production at 45 nm in 2007 [@mistry2007]
high-k gate dielectrics were the first big ALD product [@george2010]

spec.tool: ALD chamber in a gate-stack cluster
spec.purpose: Thin the equivalent oxide without the leakage

params.name: First volume high-k metal gate node

spec.ooc: Leakage high: the film is too thin or has pinholes

steps.deep: A hafnium-based insulator has a much higher dielectric constant than silicon dioxide, so it can be physically thicker for the same capacitance, which cuts tunnelling leakage [@mistry2007]. Only ALD could make it thin and even enough [@george2010].

steps.title: Measure thickness and coverage
steps.do: Measure the blanket thickness by ellipsometry, then cut a test trench and compare the film on the floor and walls with the top.
steps.check: Step coverage meets the spec for this layer.

chips.t: step coverage = thinnest wall or floor ÷ top thickness [@plummer2000]

spec.purpose: Confirm the film is thick enough everywhere
spec.control: Blanket thickness map; step coverage on test trenches
spec.ooc: Keyhole void or thin floor: change method, taper the trench or etch back and redeposit

steps.deep: If the mouth closes before the floor fills, a void is sealed inside: a keyhole. Voids raise resistance and fail early. Low-sticking CVD and ALD fill from the walls inward and stay seamless [@plummer2000].

variant.title: From sputtering to CVD to ALD
variant.lead: Each step down in trench width needed a method whose molecules reach further before they stick.

facts.t: Atomic layer epitaxy began in the 1970s for thin-film displays
ALD aluminium oxide grows about 0.1 nm per cycle
Hafnium-based high-k gate dielectrics entered volume CMOS at 45 nm in 2007
A low sticking probability gives better step coverage in CVD

variant.safety: CVD and ALD precursors are toxic, flammable or ignite in air, and the tools run hot and under vacuum. Only trained staff handle the gases.

leave_out: Sticking probability is one number per process; real precursors change it with temperature and surface.
The trench model works in molecular flow, ignoring gas-phase reactions and the boundary layer above the wafer.
No precursor, temperature or flow is given: those are institution-only.
Film stress, density, impurities and the interface layer under a high-k film are described, not modelled.

manuals.title: Make the surface flat again
manuals.subtitle: Planarization: spin-on glass in older processes, chemical mechanical polishing (CMP) today
manuals.route: Teaching CMOS (spin-on glass era) and modern logic (CMP after isolation, contacts and every copper layer)
manuals.next: Manual 9 · Device modules, Manual 10 · Damascene copper, or Manual 4A · Lithography for the next layer
manuals.intro: Every patterned layer leaves bumps, and each new layer copies them. After a few layers the surface is too uneven for the next lithography step to focus on. Planarization flattens it again: first with liquid spin-on glass, and since the 1990s with chemical mechanical polishing, which grinds the wafer flat with a pad and a slurry.
manuals.model_after: CMP follows Preston’s law [@preston1927] and the pattern-density model the Fab Journey’s CMP theatre uses [@stine1998]; tool facts come from the CMP article [@wiki_cmp].

you_need.label: Wafer with a bumpy oxide over lines

steps.title: See the problem
steps.do: Look at the wafer after deposition. The oxide copies every line underneath, so the top is a row of bumps.
steps.check: Measure the step height across the lines.

chips.t: lithography needs the surface inside the depth of focus [@wiki_cmp]

spec.purpose: Know the step height before polishing
spec.ooc: Steps too tall for the next layer: planarize

steps.deep: Each new film follows the shape under it. Without planarization the steps add up layer after layer, and a lens with a shallow depth of focus cannot image the top and bottom of a step at once [@wiki_cmp].

steps.title: Older fix: spin-on glass
steps.do: Spin a liquid glass onto the wafer like resist. It flows into the low places, then a bake turns it solid.
steps.check: Gaps are filled and the film has no cracks.

chips.t: spun, then cured in a furnace [@plummer2000]
smooths but does not fully flatten

spec.ooc: Cracks: thinner coats or a slower cure

steps.deep: Spin-on glass fills narrow gaps and rounds steps off, but it only smooths the surface locally: wide features still leave a step. It was widely used before chemical mechanical polishing took over [@plummer2000].

steps.title: Mount face down on the pad
steps.do: Hold the wafer upside down in a carrier and press it onto a rotating polishing pad wetted with slurry.
steps.check: Pad conditioned, slurry flowing, carrier pressure set.

chips.t: porous polymer pad, 30–50 µm pores [@wiki_cmp]
abrasive slurry, often cerium dioxide [@wiki_cmp]

spec.tool: CMP polisher: platen, pad, carrier, slurry arm, pad conditioner
spec.ooc: Glazed pad, slow removal: recondition the pad

steps.deep: The pad is consumed as it works and is regularly reconditioned [@wiki_cmp]. The slurry is both chemical and mechanical: its chemistry softens the surface and its abrasive particles wipe the softened layer away [@wiki_cmp].

steps.title: Polish the high spots first
steps.do: Spin pad and wafer. The pad touches the bumps first, so they wear away fastest.
steps.check: Removal rate on a monitor wafer matches the expected value.

chips.t: Preston: rate = Kₚ · P · V [@preston1927]
raised areas carry the pressure [@stine1998]

spec.ooc: Rate drifts: check pad and slurry

steps.deep: Preston’s law says removal rate is proportional to pressure times sliding speed [@preston1927]. Over a pattern the pad rests only on the high areas at first, so their local pressure is higher and they polish faster until the step is gone [@stine1998].

steps.title: Stop when it is flat
steps.do: Keep polishing until the bumps are gone and the oxide over the lines has the target thickness.
steps.check: The surface is flat within what lithography can focus on.

chips.t: brings the surface within the depth of field [@wiki_cmp]

spec.tool: CMP polisher with endpoint or timed polish
spec.purpose: Reach a flat surface at target thickness
spec.ooc: Too thin: the lines may be exposed; scrap or add oxide

steps.deep: On metal layers the polish is designed to stop on the interface between copper and oxide [@wiki_cmp], so the metal is left only inside the trenches: the damascene method.

steps.title: Mind the pattern density
steps.do: Check dense and sparse regions. Dense patterns polish more slowly, sparse ones faster, so the die is not perfectly flat.
steps.check: Thickness difference between dense and sparse areas is within limit.

chips.t: dense regions planarize more slowly [@stine1998]
fix: dummy fill in empty areas

spec.ooc: Too uneven: add dummy fill to the layout

steps.deep: Because the pad shares its pressure over the raised area, local removal depends on the layout’s pattern density [@stine1998]. Designers add dummy fill so every region has a similar density. Copper lines can also be dished below the oxide, and dense arrays eroded: both are density effects.

steps.title: Clean off the slurry
steps.do: Scrub and rinse the wafer so no slurry particles stay behind.
steps.check: Particle count after clean is within limit.

chips.t: post-CMP clean [@plummer2000]

spec.ooc: Scratches or particles: check the pad, slurry filter and cleaner

steps.deep: Slurry particles left on the wafer become defects in the next layer. CMP can also cause stress cracking, delamination at weak interfaces and corrosion from the slurry chemicals [@wiki_cmp].

variant.title: Three polishes in every modern chip
variant.lead: CMP is not one step but a family, each tuned to stop on a different material.

facts.t: Shallow trench isolation: the oxide overburden left after trench fill is polished away
Tungsten contacts and plugs are polished back to the oxide
Copper damascene: the polish stops at the copper–oxide interface
Removal rate follows pressure × speed (Preston’s law)
Pattern density sets how fast each region planarizes

tables.title: Spin-on glass versus CMP
head: Spin-on glass
CMP
rows: liquid glass spun on and cured [@plummer2000]
flat across the die, within the depth of field [@wiki_cmp]

leave_out: Removal rates, pad materials and slurries vary widely; the model uses teaching values.
Pad wear, temperature and slurry chemistry are not modelled.
Spin-on glass chemistry and cure recipes are not given.

manuals.title: Build the transistor in three dimensions
manuals.subtitle: Device modules: isolation, high-k metal gate, fins, a silicon–germanium stack, release and gate wrap
manuals.route: Modern logic: planar to FinFET to gate-all-around nanosheets
manuals.intro: A modern transistor is not a flat strip any more. To keep the gate in control of a channel only a few nanometres long, the channel was stood on edge as a fin and then split into stacked sheets that the gate wraps on every side. This manual walks through the modules that build it, each made of the operations in the earlier manuals.
manuals.model_after: The module sequence follows the multigate review by Ferain, Colinge and Colinge [@ferain2011], the DELTA fin [@hisamoto1989], Intel’s 45 nm high-k metal gate [@mistry2007] and 14 nm FinFET [@natarajan2014], and IBM’s stacked nanosheets [@loubet2017]; the sheet release follows the Fab Journey’s release theatre.

you_need.label: Lithography, etch, deposition, epitaxy and polish tools

steps.title: Isolate each transistor
steps.do: Etch shallow trenches around every active area, fill them with oxide and polish flat, so neighbouring transistors cannot talk to each other.
steps.check: Trenches filled with no voids; the surface is flat.

chips.t: shallow trench isolation replaced the older grown LOCOS oxide [@plummer2000]

spec.control: Trench depth; fill voids; step height after polish
spec.ooc: Void in the fill or dishing: rework the deposition or the polish

steps.deep: The trench is etched, lined, filled by deposition and polished back to the silicon, combining Manuals 5, 7B and 8 [@plummer2000].

steps.title: Put a high-k metal gate on a flat channel
steps.do: Grow a thin interface oxide, deposit a high-k insulator by ALD and cap it with a metal gate. This was the planar transistor’s last big change.
steps.check: Gate capacitance up, leakage down, threshold on target.

chips.t: high-k metal gates entered volume production at 45 nm in 2007 [@mistry2007]

spec.purpose: Thin the gate insulator electrically without the leakage

params.name: First volume high-k metal gate node

spec.control: Equivalent oxide thickness, gate leakage, threshold voltage
spec.ooc: Threshold off: the gate-metal work function is wrong; leakage high: the high-k film is thin

steps.deep: A higher dielectric constant gives the same capacitance from a thicker film, so electrons can no longer tunnel straight through it. Polysilicon gates were replaced by metals because they did not work with the new insulator [@mistry2007].

steps.title: Stand the channel up as a fin
steps.do: Pattern and etch narrow silicon walls, then recess the isolation oxide so the top of each wall stands free. The gate will wrap three sides.
steps.check: Fin width and height on target; fins straight.

chips.t: the DELTA fin transistor was shown in 1989 [@hisamoto1989]
14 nm FinFETs needed self-aligned double patterning [@natarajan2014]

spec.purpose: Give the gate control from three sides
spec.control: Fin width, height and pitch; fin bending
spec.ooc: Bent or thinned fins: tune the etch and the oxide recess

steps.deep: A gate on three sides holds the channel off far better than a gate on one, so leakage stays low at short lengths [@ferain2011]. Fins narrower than the lithography can print are made by spacer patterning [@natarajan2014].

steps.title: Grow a silicon–germanium stack
steps.do: For nanosheets, grow alternating layers of silicon and silicon–germanium on the wafer, then etch them into fins.
steps.check: Layer thicknesses and germanium content on target, with no defects.

chips.t: epitaxy gases are institution-only
the silicon layers become the channels; the silicon–germanium is sacrificial

spec.purpose: Build the layers that become the stacked channels
spec.ooc: Defects in the stack: the lab requalifies the reactor
