steps.deep: Each layer grows in the crystal arrangement of the one below. The silicon–germanium is there only to hold the silicon sheets apart until the gate goes in [@loubet2017]. The reactor gases are institution-only.

steps.title: Release the sheets and wrap the gate
steps.do: With the source and drain in place, remove the dummy gate, etch the silicon–germanium away selectively and fill the gaps with high-k and gate metal, so the gate surrounds every sheet.
steps.check: No silicon–germanium left; every sheet fully wrapped.

chips.t: the release etch chemistry is institution-only
inner spacers protect the source and drain while the sheets are freed

spec.tool: Selective etch and replacement-gate tools, staff only
spec.purpose: Let the gate grip each channel from every side
spec.ooc: Leftover silicon–germanium or thinned sheets: the lab adjusts the etch

steps.deep: The release etch removes silicon–germanium far faster than silicon, but not infinitely faster, so the sheet edges thin while the middle is still being freed. The Fab Journey’s release theatre computes that trade-off without giving any chemistry [@loubet2017].

steps.title: Measure the transistors
steps.do: Probe test transistors for drive current, leakage and threshold, and cut cross-sections to check every sheet.
steps.check: Drive current and leakage on target across the wafer.

chips.t: nanosheet transistors entered volume production at the 2 nm class in 2025 [@tsmc_n2]

spec.purpose: Confirm the transistors switch as designed
spec.control: On-current, off-current, threshold voltage, sheet thickness
spec.ooc: Threshold shifted: sheets thinned in the release; leakage: incomplete wrap

steps.deep: Thinner sheets raise the threshold voltage and cut the drive current, so sheet thickness measured in cross-section is tied back to the electrical results [@loubet2017].

variant.title: From a flat gate to a gate on every side
variant.lead: Each generation gave the gate more grip on the channel so the transistor could keep shrinking.

facts.t: High-k metal gates replaced oxide and polysilicon at 45 nm in 2007
The DELTA fin transistor was shown in 1989
Stacked nanosheets were shown as FinFET’s successor in 2017
Nanosheet transistors entered volume production at the 2 nm class in 2025

variant.safety: Epitaxy gases and the selective release etch are institution-only; every module runs in staff-operated tools.

leave_out: The pictures are schematic: real fins and sheets are a few nanometres thick and drawn far larger here.
Source and drain epitaxy, inner spacers and the replacement-gate sequence are named, not drawn step by step.
No epitaxy gas, etch chemistry or recipe is given: those are institution-only.
Strain, work-function tuning and backside power delivery are left out.

manuals.title: Wire the chip in copper
manuals.subtitle: Dual damascene: insulator, trench, barrier, seed, plate, polish, measure
manuals.route: Modern logic: every wiring layer above the transistors
manuals.next: Manual 11 · Probe and package (after the last layer)
manuals.intro: Copper cannot be etched cleanly like aluminium, so it is wired the other way round. Grooves are cut into the insulator first, lined, filled with copper and polished flat, leaving copper only in the grooves, like an inlaid damascene sword. A modern chip repeats this for a dozen or more layers.
manuals.model_after: The wiring follows the dual-damascene scheme [@kaanta1991] and the first full copper process [@edelstein1997]; line resistivity follows the size-effect models used by the Fab Journey’s copper theatre [@mayadas1970] with mean free paths from Gall [@gall2016]; polishing follows the pattern-density model [@stine1998].

you_need.label: Dielectric deposition, etch and lithography tools
Barrier and seed chamber, plating cell (staff-run), polisher

steps.title: Lay down the insulator
steps.do: Deposit the insulating layer that the wires will sit in, often a low-k film that lowers the capacitance between neighbouring lines.
steps.check: Thickness and dielectric constant on monitors are on target.

chips.t: a lower dielectric constant cuts the RC delay of every wire [@plummer2000]

spec.purpose: Make the layer the wires are inlaid into
spec.ooc: Dielectric constant high: the porous film was damaged; requalify

steps.deep: Porous low-k films are fragile, and etching or stripping resist can raise their dielectric constant again, so the later steps are kept gentle [@plummer2000].

steps.title: Pattern and etch the trenches and vias
steps.do: Print the via holes and the line trenches with lithography and etch both into the insulator, so one fill later makes the vias and the lines together.
steps.check: Trench width and depth are on target.

chips.t: vias and lines filled in one step: dual damascene [@kaanta1991]

spec.purpose: Cut the shape of the wiring into the insulator
spec.ooc: Trench too wide or too deep: rework before any metal goes in

steps.deep: The ratio of depth to width, the aspect ratio, decides how hard the next steps are: the barrier and seed must reach the bottom corners, and the plating must fill without a seam [@kaanta1991].

steps.title: Line it with a barrier and a seed
steps.do: Coat every surface with a thin barrier that copper cannot cross, then a thin copper seed for the plating to grow from.
steps.check: The barrier and seed are continuous down to the trench floor.

chips.t: copper must never touch silicon or oxide: the liner keeps it in [@edelstein1997]
the barrier conducts poorly, so it is dead area in a narrow line [@gall2016]

spec.tool: PVD or ALD barrier and seed chamber
spec.purpose: Seal the copper in and give plating a start
spec.control: Sheet resistance of the seed; coverage on test trenches
spec.ooc: Gaps at the bottom corners: voids later in the plated line

steps.deep: Copper diffuses quickly into silicon dioxide and silicon, where it ruins transistors, so the barrier wraps every line. The barrier must be thin, because in a 20 nm line every nanometre of it takes conductor away [@edelstein1997; @gall2016].

steps.title: Fill by electroplating
steps.do: Trained staff run the plating cell. Copper grows from the seed until every trench is full, and a little beyond.
steps.check: Every trench is filled with no seam; the overburden covers the wafer.

chips.t: the plating bath is institution-only
additives make the trench fill from the bottom up

spec.ooc: Seam or void in the fill: the lab adjusts the bath

steps.deep: Additives in the bath slow growth at the trench mouth and speed it at the floor, so the trench fills from the bottom up without a seam [@edelstein1997]. The bath chemistry is process know-how and stays with the lab; nothing about it is given here.

steps.title: Polish back to the insulator
steps.do: Polish away the copper and barrier on top until only the copper in the trenches remains.
steps.check: The field is clear of metal and no lines are shorted.

chips.t: removal rate rises with pressure and speed: Preston’s law [@preston1927]
wide lines dish and dense arrays erode [@stine1998]

spec.purpose: Leave copper only where the wiring belongs
spec.control: Endpoint from friction or reflected light; dishing and erosion on test structures
spec.ooc: Residual copper between lines: polish more; dished lines: tune the pad and slurry

steps.deep: Copper is softer than the insulator, so wide lines are polished below the surface (dishing) and dense regions lose insulator too (erosion). Both thin the line and raise its resistance [@stine1998].

steps.title: Measure the wires
steps.do: Probe test structures: long serpentines for resistance, interleaved combs for shorts.
steps.check: Line resistance and comb leakage within limits.

chips.t: a 10 nm copper line conducts about three times worse than bulk would suggest: surfaces and grain boundaries scatter electrons [@mayadas1970]

spec.purpose: Confirm the wiring conducts and is isolated
spec.ooc: Resistance high: thin line, dishing or voids; leakage: copper residue

steps.deep: Narrow lines scatter electrons at their surfaces and grain boundaries, so resistivity rises well above the bulk value just as the cross-section shrinks. That is why ruthenium and other metals with short mean free paths are being considered for the tightest layers [@gall2016].

variant.title: From aluminium to copper
variant.lead: Copper conducts better and resists electromigration, but it needed a whole new way of patterning.

facts.t: Bulk copper resistivity is about 1.7 µΩ·cm, aluminium about 2.65
Dual damascene fills vias and lines in one step
IBM announced full copper wiring in production CMOS in 1997
Thin films conduct worse because electrons scatter at grain boundaries and surfaces

variant.safety: Plating baths, the acids around them and polishing slurries are handled only by trained staff, and copper must be kept out of every tool that touches bare silicon.

leave_out: The cross-section shows one trench; dual damascene cuts a via and a line in one opening.
Resistivity follows the site’s size-effect model; real lines also depend on grain size after the anneal and on the barrier material.
No plating chemistry, current or polishing slurry is given: those are institution-only.
Electromigration and stress voiding are covered by the electromigration simulator, not this manual.

manuals.title: Find the good dies and package them
manuals.subtitle: Back end: probe test structures, test every die, map, saw, pick, bond and test again
manuals.route: Every route: the last steps before a chip leaves the fab
manuals.next: The finished chip: back to the Fab Journey
manuals.intro: A finished wafer holds anything from a handful to hundreds of chips, and some are dead. Probing finds them, a saw cuts the wafer apart, and only the good dies are packaged and wired to the outside world. No test catches every fault, so the last question is how many bad chips slip through.
manuals.model_after: Yield follows Stapper’s negative-binomial model [@stapper1973] and Murphy’s cost argument [@murphy1964]; escaped defects follow Williams and Brown [@williams1981]; the teaching-run results come from its electrical characterization [@cleanroom_run_char2024]. The probe theatre computes all of it.

you_need.label: Dicing saw, die picker, wire bonder

steps.title: Probe the test structures
steps.do: Lower needles onto the test resistors, capacitors and transistors beside the dies and measure them first. They tell you whether the process worked before any chip is tested.
steps.check: Threshold voltages and sheet resistances are inside their limits.

chips.t: teaching run: 8 of 9 test MOSFETs switched [@cleanroom_run_char2024]
test structures sit in the scribe lanes

spec.tool: Wafer prober with a parametric analyser
spec.purpose: Check the process before the product
spec.ooc: Parameters out of range: hold the lot and tell process engineering

steps.deep: Parametric tests measure the process, not the design. In the teaching run they showed thresholds pulled negative by charge in the oxide, and one short-channel device that never turned off [@cleanroom_run_char2024].

steps.title: Test every die
steps.do: Step the wafer under the probe card die by die and run the test patterns. Each die passes or is put in a failure bin.
steps.check: Every die has a result.

chips.t: fault coverage: the share of modelled faults the patterns catch [@williams1981]

spec.control: Fault coverage and test time per die
spec.ooc: A whole region fails: look for a tool problem, not random defects

steps.deep: Scan chains let a few pins reach millions of internal flip-flops, so patterns can be generated automatically for a fault model. Test time costs money, so patterns that fail bad dies early run first [@williams1981].

steps.title: Make the wafer map
steps.do: Colour each die by its result. The pattern of failures says as much as their number.
steps.check: The map is saved with the lot record.

chips.t: Y = (1 + A·D₀/α)^(−α) [@stapper1973]
big dies catch more defects [@murphy1964]

spec.control: Yield per wafer and per lot
spec.ooc: Rings, scratches or clusters: trace them to a tool

steps.deep: Defects cluster, so the negative-binomial model with a clustering parameter α fits real wafers better than a random scatter [@stapper1973]. Murphy showed in 1964 that yield and die size together set the cost of a chip [@murphy1964].

steps.title: Saw the wafer apart
steps.do: Mount the wafer on tape in a frame and cut along the scribe lanes with a diamond blade. The dies stay on the tape.
steps.check: Clean cuts; no chipped die edges.

chips.t: the cut destroys the test structures in the lanes
some wafers are cut by laser instead

spec.ooc: Chipped edges: slow the feed or change the blade

steps.deep: Cooling water carries heat and debris away. An edge chip that looks harmless can grow into a crack once the die is stressed in its package.

steps.title: Pick the good dies
steps.do: The picker reads the wafer map and lifts only the dies that passed. Each is inspected before it goes into a tray or onto a package.
steps.check: Only passing dies leave the tape.

chips.t: cost per good die is wafer cost divided by good dies [@murphy1964]

spec.ooc: Picker and map disagree: stop and re-align

steps.deep: Chiplets and 3D stacks join several dies in one package, so a single bad die wastes all the good ones beside it: every die must be known good before it is assembled [@tsmc_3dfabric].

steps.title: Bond wires to the pads
steps.do: Glue the die into its package, then join each pad to a package lead with a fine wire.
steps.check: Every wire passes a pull test on samples.

chips.t: gold or copper wire, welded by heat and ultrasound
advanced packages use bumps instead [@tsmc_3dfabric]

spec.purpose: Connect the die to the outside
spec.ooc: Weak bonds: clean the pads and recheck the bond settings

steps.deep: Wire bonds have joined chips to packages since the planar era. Modern high-performance packages replace them with solder bumps or direct copper-to-copper bonding between stacked dies [@tsmc_3dfabric].

steps.title: Test again, packaged
steps.do: Test the packaged part at speed and temperature. Assembly can damage a die, and some faults are only reachable through the package.
steps.check: The part passes, and is marked and shipped.

chips.t: defect level DL = 1 − Y^(1 − T) [@williams1981]
90 % coverage lets about ten times more bad parts through than 99 % [@williams1981]

spec.control: Defect level in parts per million
spec.ooc: Escapes at the customer: raise test coverage

steps.deep: Williams and Brown showed that the share of bad parts that pass the test depends on both yield and fault coverage, DL = 1 − Y^(1 − T) [@williams1981]. The probe theatre lets you change both.

variant.title: How many bad chips slip through
variant.lead: Yield says how many dies are good. Test coverage says how many of the bad ones you catch.

facts.t: Murphy related die size to yield and cost in 1964
Stapper modelled defect clustering with the negative binomial in 1973
Williams and Brown linked fault coverage to the defect level customers see in 1981
Teaching run: 8 of 9 test MOSFETs switched; the shortest never turned off

leave_out: Every defect is treated as a killer; real tests bin dies by speed and repair memory with spare rows.
The defect-level formula assumes faults are equally likely and independent.
Saw, pick and bond are drawn, not modelled; their own yield losses are left out.
Burn-in, reliability screens and packaging stress are only mentioned.

manuals.title: Make a transistor on glass
manuals.subtitle: An oxide thin-film transistor (IGZO): another process family, built at low temperature with no crystal at all
manuals.route: Displays and flexible electronics; compare the Fab Journey’s process-family table
manuals.intro: Not every transistor starts from a silicon crystal. The screen you are reading is driven by thin-film transistors built on glass, layer by deposited layer. Amorphous oxide semiconductors such as indium–gallium–zinc oxide (IGZO) can even be made at room temperature on plastic. This manual builds a bottom-gate oxide transistor with the operations from the earlier manuals.
manuals.model_after: The device follows the thin-film transistor of Weimer [@weimer1962] and the room-temperature amorphous-oxide transistor of Nomura et al. [@nomura2004]; the flexible processor example is Ozer et al. [@ozer2024]; deposition and patterning follow Manuals 4A, 5 and 7B and Plummer, Deal and Griffin [@plummer2000].

steps.title: Pattern a metal gate on the glass
steps.do: Deposit a metal film on the glass and pattern it into gate lines. The gate sits at the bottom of this transistor.
steps.check: Gate lines continuous; edges smooth.

chips.t: the first thin-film transistor was shown in 1962 [@weimer1962]

spec.purpose: Make the gate first, on an insulating sheet
spec.ooc: Rough edges: they will thin the insulator above them

steps.deep: With no crystal to build on, every layer is deposited. Putting the gate first lets the semiconductor go on last, over a smooth insulator [@weimer1962].

steps.title: Deposit the gate insulator
steps.do: Cover everything with a thin insulating film by CVD or sputtering.
steps.check: Thickness and leakage on target.

chips.t: deposited, not grown: there is no silicon to oxidise [@plummer2000]

spec.purpose: Separate the gate from the channel
spec.ooc: Leaky capacitors: pinholes; deposit thicker or cleaner

steps.deep: On silicon the best insulator is grown from the wafer itself. On glass it has to be deposited, so its quality sets much of the transistor’s behaviour [@plummer2000].

steps.title: Sputter the oxide semiconductor
steps.do: Sputter a thin amorphous IGZO film over the gate and pattern it into islands. It works without being crystallised, and it can be made at room temperature.
steps.check: Island thickness and resistance on monitors on target.

chips.t: amorphous oxide transistors made at room temperature on plastic [@nomura2004]

spec.purpose: Lay the channel over the gate
spec.control: Film thickness; oxygen content set by the lab
spec.ooc: Channel too conductive: the transistor will not switch off

steps.deep: Electrons in these oxides travel through overlapping metal orbitals, which work even when the atoms are disordered, so the film needs no crystal and no high temperature [@nomura2004].

steps.title: Add source and drain
steps.do: Deposit and pattern metal over the ends of each island, leaving a gap over the gate: that gap is the channel length.
steps.check: Gap length on target; contacts ohmic.

chips.t: the gap between source and drain is the channel length [@weimer1962]

spec.ooc: Gap bridged: short; rework the etch

steps.deep: The etch that separates source from drain must not eat the thin semiconductor below it, so the chemistries are chosen for selectivity, as in Manual 5 [@plummer2000].

steps.title: Seal and anneal
steps.do: Cover the transistor with a protective film and give it a mild bake, which steadies the oxide semiconductor.
steps.check: Threshold stable under bias stress.

chips.t: sealing keeps moisture and oxygen from shifting the threshold [@nomura2004]

spec.ooc: Threshold drifts: improve the seal or the bake

steps.deep: Oxide semiconductors respond to the gases around them, so an unsealed transistor drifts. The bake stays far below what a silicon furnace uses, which is why plastic sheets survive it [@nomura2004].

steps.title: Measure and compare
steps.do: Probe the transfer curve: drain current against gate voltage. Compare its on–off ratio and threshold with the silicon transistors in the other manuals.
steps.check: On–off ratio and threshold within spec across the sheet.

chips.t: a bendable RISC-V processor was built from 0.6 µm IGZO transistors [@ozer2024]

spec.control: Transfer curve: threshold, on–off ratio, subthreshold slope
spec.ooc: Low on-current: thick insulator or poor contacts

steps.deep: Oxide transistors are far slower than crystalline silicon but cheap, transparent and buildable on anything flat, which is why they drive displays and are starting to carry simple processors on plastic [@ozer2024].

variant.title: No crystal, no furnace
variant.lead: Thin-film transistors trade speed for building on glass and plastic.

facts.t: Weimer showed the thin-film transistor in 1962
Amorphous oxide transistors were made at room temperature on plastic in 2004
A bendable RISC-V processor used 0.6 µm IGZO transistors in 2024
Every layer is deposited, because there is no silicon to grow oxide from

variant.safety: Sputter and CVD tools run under vacuum and some CVD gases are institution-only; the etches are staff-run.

leave_out: The cross-section is schematic; real films are tens of nanometres thick.
No sputter target composition, gas mix or etch is given: those are set by the lab.
Bias-stress drift, light sensitivity and contact resistance are described, not modelled.
Top-gate and self-aligned oxide transistors, and low-temperature polysilicon, are left out.

manuals.title: Make a planar transistor the 1959 way
manuals.subtitle: Hoerni’s planar process: grow oxide, open a window, predeposit, drive in under the oxide, evaporate leads, test breakdown
manuals.route: Historical planar process, the ancestor of every integrated circuit
manuals.intro: Before 1959 transistors were mesas: bumps etched out of the silicon with their junctions exposed at the sides, where dirt and moisture spoiled them. Jean Hoerni kept the oxide on. Dopant went in through a window, spread sideways under the oxide edge and ended under protecting glass, and the wafer stayed flat. Robert Noyce then ran aluminium leads over that oxide, which made the integrated circuit possible.
manuals.model_after: The sequence follows Hoerni’s patent [@hoerni1962] and Noyce’s lead structure [@noyce_patent], with oxide masking from Frosch and Derick [@frosch1957]; breakdown of the flat junction and its curved edge follows Sze and Gibbons [@sze_gibbons1966; @sze_gibbons_curv1966], as computed by the Fab Journey’s planar theatre; the history follows Riordan and Hoddeson [@riordan1997].

steps.title: Grow the masking oxide
steps.do: Oxidise the whole wafer in a furnace. The glass will block the dopant everywhere except where a window is opened.
steps.check: Oxide thickness even across the wafer.

chips.t: silicon dioxide masks the common dopants [@frosch1957]
a grown oxide also quiets the silicon surface [@atalla1959]

spec.purpose: Cover the wafer in a dopant mask
spec.control: Oxide thickness by colour or ellipsometry
spec.ooc: Pinholes in the oxide: dopant leaks through; regrow

steps.deep: Frosch and Derick found in 1957 that a grown oxide blocks boron and phosphorus, and Atalla showed that it also stabilises the silicon surface [@frosch1957; @atalla1959]. Hoerni put both to work.

steps.title: Open a window
steps.do: Print a window with photoresist and etch the oxide away inside it. Its edge sets where the junction will meet the surface.
steps.check: Window clean to the silicon, edges sharp.

chips.t: the window edge decides where the junction surfaces [@hoerni1962]

spec.purpose: Let dopant in only where it belongs
spec.control: Window size; no oxide left in it
spec.ooc: Oxide left in the window: etch again

steps.deep: Pattern and etch follow Manuals 4A and 5. The etch chemistry for oxide is institution-only.

steps.title: Predeposit the dopant
steps.do: Trained staff run the dopant source in a furnace. A thin, heavily doped skin forms in the window only.
steps.check: Sheet resistance of a monitor wafer on target.

chips.t: the dopant source is institution-only
the oxide stops it everywhere else

spec.purpose: Set the dose of dopant in the window
spec.ooc: Monitor out of range: the lab adjusts the source

steps.deep: A constant-source predeposition fixes the dose, as in Manual 6A. The source chemistry stays with the lab; nothing about it is given here.

steps.title: Drive in under the oxide edge
steps.do: Heat again with the source removed. The dopant spreads down and sideways, so the junction curves up and meets the surface under the oxide, not in the open.
steps.check: Junction depth on a bevelled monitor on target.

chips.t: the junction ends under protecting oxide [@hoerni1962]
sideways spread is about 0.8 of the depth [@plummer2000]

spec.purpose: Bury the junction edge under glass
spec.ooc: Junction too shallow: the edge curves sharply and breaks down early

steps.deep: Because the dopant moves sideways about as far as down, the junction reaches the surface beneath the oxide edge. That is the whole trick: the edge, where mesa transistors failed, is sealed from the start [@hoerni1962; @riordan1997].

steps.title: Evaporate aluminium leads over the oxide
steps.do: Open contact holes, evaporate aluminium over the whole wafer and pattern it, so the leads run across the oxide to the junctions.
steps.check: Leads continuous; contacts ohmic.

chips.t: leads over the oxide connected devices on one chip [@noyce_patent]

spec.purpose: Wire the device without touching bare silicon
spec.ooc: Open lead over the oxide step: thicker metal or a gentler step

steps.deep: Because the planar wafer is flat and covered in glass, a metal film can run over it from one device to the next. Noyce’s 1959 patent did exactly that, and the integrated circuit followed [@noyce_patent].

steps.title: Test the breakdown
steps.do: Reverse-bias the junction on a curve tracer and find the voltage where current suddenly rises. The curved edge breaks down before the flat floor.
steps.check: Breakdown above the specification.

chips.t: the curved edge breaks down first [@sze_gibbons_curv1966]
1 h at 1100 °C: flat 347 V, edge 150 V in the model [@sze_gibbons1966]

spec.purpose: Confirm the junction holds its voltage
spec.ooc: Early breakdown: shallow junction or a damaged edge

steps.deep: The field crowds at the curved edge, whose radius is about the junction depth, so it avalanches before the flat floor. A deeper drive-in gives a gentler curve: four hours at 1150 °C raise the edge from 43 to 60 % of the flat value in the planar theatre [@sze_gibbons_curv1966].

variant.title: From mesa to planar to the integrated circuit
variant.lead: Keeping the oxide on made transistors reliable, flat and wireable on one chip.

facts.t: Frosch and Derick found in 1957 that silicon dioxide masks dopant diffusion
Hoerni filed the planar process in 1959
Noyce filed aluminium leads over the oxide in 1959
A grown oxide stabilises the silicon surface

variant.safety: Diffusion sources are institution-only and furnaces run near 1100 °C; every step here runs in a staff-operated lab.

leave_out: The junction edge is a cylinder of radius equal to the depth; real edges also have corners, which break down even earlier.
Breakdown uses Sze and Gibbons’ formulas for a one-sided abrupt junction; a diffused junction is graded.
No dopant source or furnace setting beyond the model example is given: the source is institution-only.
Surface charge in the oxide, which troubled early planar devices, is described, not modelled.

intro: Each manual takes one process step by step, like a building-brick instruction book: a picture per step with the new part outlined, a parts list and a check. Switch to Engineer or Process engineer for the operation specification behind each step, cited to public sources.
